reviews.review:
An extremely goofy, entertaining, fun, and frustrating game all in one. I can happily recommend this on sale to just about anybody, but it does have its problems. Keep reading to find out more, though I do discuss various mechanics. Oh, and beware arachnophobes! [b] This game has a lot of giant spiders in it [/b]; avoid if you have a phobia of spiders!

EDF5 is a strange mix of a couple of genres, though the best way I can describe it is class-based third-person horde shooter with a lot of campy B-movie action flick comedy moments sprinkled in for good measure. Despite initial appearances, a slow start, and a relatively steep learning curve, the game is fresh and easy to get into once you manage past the first 10-15 missions. Players starting with the Ranger class will feel a distinct sense of familiarity with its more conventional weapon variety, including assault rifles, machine guns, special weapons like grenade launchers, and rockets/missiles. Players wishing to experience the true uniqueness of EDF may pick any of the other three classes, which each play very differently. Combat variety is one of this game's strengths, and in a 4-man squad, maintains its fun factor for potentially hundreds of hours. Though it has more faults than you might suspect.

I can easily recommend this game on a steep sale, especially if you can compel a few buddies to get it with you. But be prepared for moments of intense frustration and confusion lest you have a classic gamer moment. 

For one, the mission design can be extremely repetitive, but this comes down to the 110 total missions playable in the campaign. Many of them are generic repeats that introduce nothing interesting beyond maintaining the admittedly fun gameplay loop. Despite that, the game's difficulty varies wildly throughout the campaign, spiking and falling off within the same span of 2-3 missions. This is only really problematic due to the game's extremely limiting and confusing level limit and armor limit mechanics.

A weapon's level is a static minimum requirement, and each mission has its own maximum level restriction. Until you finish the campaign, these limiters cannot be disabled, rendering cool new weapons useless when brought back down to a lower level. Armor is the game's health, acquired through red crates dropped by enemies in-mission, and also have a limiter, though this one is substantially more forgiving. The real problem, however, lies in the game's weapon acquisition system.

Weapons are acquired from green crates also dropped by slain enemies, and each crate has a randomized weapon inside. Already we run into an issue. Not only are the weapons totally randomized, they are also in specific level brackets, meaning if you want a level 20 weapon upgraded, you cannot grind missions too far below or above that bracket as that weapon simply will not be in the randomized pool. On top of that, duplicate weapons improve a random statistic of the weapon up to a certain threshold represented by a star. What this ultimately entails is that grinding for a specific weapon or weapon levels is entirely RNG dependent and can take hours to achieve the results you want. Some weapons are utterly useless until upgraded, such as missile launchers having an initial 3.3 second lockon, but at max level, the lockon is reduced to 0.13 seconds. In my opinion, this is a giant, gaping hole in the progression system that can be extremely frustrating even when the game is being generous.

Now that I've thoroughly torn asunder the progression system and mission redundancy, why do I recommend this game?

When the game works, it is really like no other game. Slaying countless giant insects or monsters, blowing up enormous flying saucers, laughing at the extremely campy translation and dub work, all of it just oozes personality and fun. When the game's balance is just right between enemy variety, number, and your own kit and upgrades, it's one of the most satisfying slaughterfest games I've played in recent memory. Much of the game's glaring faults can be at least conveniently forgotten about when those magical moments happen, and frankly, they happen a lot. If you aren't sure on picking it up even on sale, I recommend trying Earth Defense Force 4.1; it's a lot like this and a hell of a lot cheaper. Absolutely recommend this gem of a game to anybody in the mood to blow something up with their main course of balls to the wall, high-octane action camp fun. 

12/10 on the fun factor. Probably like a 7/10 overall. Grab it on sale; you really won't regret it.
